To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the increase in HDL-bound Et may serve as a protection against endotoxicity, and the addition of ethanol may impair the binding capacity of HDL to Et.
the Et clearance in blood is prolonged in acute ethanol-loaded rats but is faster in chronic ethanol-loaded ones, and the HDL-bound Et is increased in both acute and chronic alcohol-fed rats.
the Et clearance in rats was prolonged in acute alcohol loading, and the amount was markedly increased in albumin and HD L.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of HDL and serum albumin in the clearance of endotoxin in rats with chronic ethanol loading.
the role of albumins and HDLs in endotoxin clearance and endotoxicity in acute and chronic ethanol-loaded rats.
the role of albumins and HDLs as Et-binding proteins and the possible mechanism for the increase in the Et-binding capacity of these proteins in chronic ethanol-loaded rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chronic ethanol loading may induce a protective mechanism against endotoxemia, and that the protective mechanism may be overwhelmed by a high-dose ethanol loading.
the role of HDL as an Et-binding protein may be more important than that of albumin in rats with acute or chronic alcohol loading.
in the chronic alcohol-loaded rats with an additional high-dose ethanol load, the impaired Et clearance and inactivation may result in increased endotoxemia and endotoxicity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Et binding and inactivating system is altered in rats with chronic ethanol loading and that the alteration may lead to the increased endotoxicity in rats when an addition of a large amount of alcohol is given.
the increase of endotoxin binding to high-density lipoproteins and albumins in the liver may serve as a mechanism to protect against endotoxemia in chronic ethanol-loaded animals.

the increased Et-binding capacity of albumin and/or HDL is a protective mechanism against endotoxin in the chronic ethanol-fed rat, and the addition of ethanol to these rats leads to impaired Et binding, which finally results in increased endotoxicities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of HDL and its interaction with albumin is critical to the development of alcoholic liver disease.
alcohol consumption increases the binding of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to HDL.

chronic alcohol loading can induce the increase in Et- binding capacity of albumin and especially HDL, and the additional high-dose alcohol may impair Et binding and inactivate, which may finally lead to the increased endotoxicity and liver injury.
